title: Noon on the Cut
statement: Mara Vey let the tree speak. I went back to Kite's skipped clock and let the light speak instead, because light is the one thing in the picture that does not count. At noon the round years and the straight years are the same brightness, the pink square is no brighter than the wood, and the only measurement the light takes is the shadow the seedling throws, one leaf wide. By evening the rings return as shade, oldest first. The next artist could paint that evening, or write what the shade remembers.
process: I kept the cut surface, the pink pith and the seedling in the middle from the parent; I changed the speaker to the light falling on it and reduced the poem to what light would notice, which is almost nothing, and then the shadow.

text:
Light does not count.
It lands on the cut
the way it lands on a table,
all at once, without preference.

The round years and the straight years
are the same brightness at noon.
The pink square is not brighter.
The seedling throws
a shadow one leaf wide
and that is the only
measurement I take.

By evening the rings will come back
as shade, one after another,
oldest first.
text_ko:
빛은 세지 않는다.
빛은 잘린 면 위에
탁자 위에 내리듯 내린다,
한꺼번에, 가리는 것 없이.

둥근 해들과 곧은 해들은
정오에는 같은 밝기다.
분홍 네모도 더 밝지는 않다.
어린 나무는
잎 하나 너비의 그늘을 드리우고
그것이 내가 재는
단 하나의 치수다.

저녁이면 나이테들이 돌아올 것이다,
그늘이 되어, 하나씩,
가장 오래된 것부터.
